lessons.title: Noun Classes
lessons.explanation: Swahili is a Bantu language, and instead of grammatical gender it groups nouns into 'noun classes' by prefix. The M-/WA- class is for people (mtu 'person' → watu 'people'); the M-/MI- class is often for plants and objects (mti 'tree' → miti 'trees'). Every adjective and verb in a sentence must agree with the noun's class.
examples: mtu (person) → watu (people) — M-/WA- class
mti (tree) → miti (trees) — M-/MI- class
kitabu (book) → vitabu (books) — KI-/VI- class
mtoto (child) → watoto (children) — M-/WA- class
lessons.tip: Unlike Hindi, Urdu, or Bangla, Swahili has no masculine/feminine gender — noun class (not sex) drives all agreement.

quiz.question: What determines agreement of adjectives and verbs in Swahili?

lessons.title: Verb Structure — Subject Prefix + Tense Marker + Stem
lessons.explanation: A Swahili verb is built from: subject prefix + tense marker + verb stem. Ninasoma = Ni- (I) + -na- (present) + -soma (read) = 'I am reading / I read'.
examples: Ninasoma. (Ni-na-soma.) — I am reading.
Anasoma. (A-na-soma.) — He/she is reading.
Tunasoma. (Tu-na-soma.) — We are reading.
Wanasoma. (Wa-na-soma.) — They are reading.
lessons.tip: Learn the subject prefixes (ni-, u-, a-, tu-, m-, wa-) first — they appear at the start of almost every verb.

quiz.question: In 'Ninasoma', what does 'Ni-' represent?

lessons.title: Tense Markers — -na-, -li-, -ta-
lessons.explanation: Swahili marks tense with an infix right after the subject prefix: -na- (present), -li- (past), -ta- (future).
examples: Ninasoma. — I read/am reading. (present, -na-)
Nilisoma. — I read (past). (-li-)
Nitasoma. — I will read. (-ta-)
Alisoma kitabu. — He/she read a book. (past, -li-)
lessons.tip: Swap only the tense infix (-na-/-li-/-ta-) to change tense — the subject prefix and verb stem stay the same.

quiz.question: Which infix marks the future tense in Swahili?

lessons.title: Word Order — SVO
lessons.explanation: Unlike Hindi, Urdu, and Bangla (all SOV), Swahili follows Subject-Verb-Object word order, much like English.
examples: Mimi ninasoma kitabu. — I am reading a book. (Subject-Verb-Object)
Rafiki yangu anapenda muziki. — My friend likes music.
Watoto wanacheza mpira. — The children are playing ball.
Mama anapika chakula. — Mother is cooking food.
lessons.tip: Because Swahili word order matches English (SVO), many learners find sentence structure easier than Hindi/Urdu's SOV.

quiz.question: What word order does Swahili use?

lessons.title: Object Markers (Infixes)
lessons.explanation: Swahili can insert an object marker right before the verb stem to mean 'him/her/it/them' without needing a separate pronoun: Ninampenda = Ni-na-m-penda = I-present-him/her-love = 'I love him/her'.
examples: Ninampenda. (Ni-na-m-penda.) — I love him/her.
Tunawapenda. (Tu-na-wa-penda.) — We love them.
Anakisoma kitabu. (A-na-ki-soma.) — He/she is reading it (the book).
Ninakiona. (Ni-na-ki-ona.) — I see it.
lessons.tip: The object marker's shape depends on the noun class of the thing being referred to, just like subject prefixes.

quiz.question: In 'Ninampenda', what does '-m-' refer to?

lessons.title: Possessive Pronouns and Adjectives
lessons.explanation: Swahili possessives are formed with a class-agreeing prefix plus a possessive root (-angu 'my', -ako 'your', -ake 'his/her', -etu 'our', -enu 'your pl.', -ao 'their'). The prefix matches the class of the noun possessed: kitabu changu (my book, KI- class uses ch-), mtoto wangu (my child, M-/WA- class uses w-).
examples: kitabu changu — my book (KI-/VI- class)
mtoto wangu — my child (M-/WA- class)
nyumba yangu — my house (N- class)
vitabu vyako — your books (KI-/VI- class, plural)
lessons.tip: Learn the possessive root (-angu, -ako, -ake...) once, then just swap the class prefix to match the noun.

quiz.question: In 'kitabu changu', what does 'changu' mean?
Which possessive root means 'our'?

lessons.title: Question Formation
lessons.explanation: Swahili yes/no questions can be formed simply with rising intonation, or by adding je at the end of the sentence (or Je, at the start). Wh-questions use words like nani (who), nini (what), wapi (where), lini (when), gani (which), and namna gani / vipi (how).
examples: Unaenda wapi? — Where are you going?
Jina lako ni nani? — What is your name? (literally 'is who')
Utakuja lini? — When will you come?
Unafanya nini? — What are you doing?
lessons.tip: Most Swahili question words replace the answer's position in the sentence rather than moving to the front, unlike English.

quiz.question: Which word means 'where' in Swahili?
Which word means 'when'?

lessons.title: Demonstratives — 'This/That' Agreement
lessons.explanation: Swahili demonstratives ('this', 'that') change their prefix to agree with the noun's class, just like adjectives and verbs. For the M-/WA- (person) class: huyu (this person), hawa (these people). For the KI-/VI- class: hiki (this thing), vile (those things, far).
examples: mtu huyu — this person (M-/WA- class)
watu hawa — these people (M-/WA- class, plural)
kitabu hiki — this book (KI-/VI- class)
vitabu vile — those books (KI-/VI- class, plural, far)
lessons.tip: Swahili demonstratives have three degrees: 'this' (huyu/hiki...), 'that' already mentioned (huyo/hicho...), and 'that' far away (yule/kile...).

quiz.question: Which demonstrative correctly means 'this person'?
What determines the form of a Swahili demonstrative?

lessons.title: Noun Class Agreement Across a Sentence
lessons.explanation: Adjectives and verbs must agree with a noun's class throughout the sentence. For the M-/WA- (people) class: mtu mzuri anasoma ('the good person is reading') — mzuri and anasoma both carry the class-agreeing prefixes. For the M-/MI- class: mti mzuri unaanguka ('the good tree is falling') uses different agreement markers.
examples: Mtu mzuri anasoma. — The good person is reading. (M-/WA- class: m-/a-)
Watu wazuri wanasoma. — The good people are reading. (plural: wa-/wa-)
Kitabu kizuri kinasomwa. — The good book is being read. (KI-/VI- class: ki-/ki-)
Vitabu vizuri vinasomwa. — The good books are being read. (plural: vi-/vi-)
lessons.tip: Memorize noun classes in pairs (singular/plural) — each pair has its own consistent set of agreement prefixes.

quiz.question: In 'Kitabu kizuri kinasomwa', which noun class is being used?

lessons.title: Future Tense (-ta-)
lessons.explanation: The Swahili future tense uses the infix -ta- between the subject prefix and verb stem: Nitasoma (Ni-ta-soma) = I will read. This mirrors the -na-/-li- pattern already used for present and past.
examples: Nitasoma kitabu. — I will read a book.
Atakuja kesho. — He/she will come tomorrow.
Tutaenda sokoni. — We will go to the market.
Watafika saa tatu. — They will arrive at nine o'clock.
lessons.tip: -ta- always slots into the same position as -na- and -li- — subject prefix + -ta- + stem.

quiz.question: Which infix marks future tense?
What does 'Atakuja' mean?

lessons.title: Subjunctive Mood (-e ending)
lessons.explanation: The Swahili subjunctive replaces the final -a of the verb with -e, and drops the tense infix. It is used for commands, suggestions, purposes ('so that'), and after verbs like 'want': Twende! (Let's go!), Ninataka asome (I want him/her to read).
examples: Twende sasa! — Let's go now! (subjunctive)
Ninataka usome kitabu. — I want you to read a book.
Aje mapema ili tuanze. — Let him come early so that we can start.
Usiende huko. — Don't go there. (negative subjunctive)
lessons.tip: Spot the subjunctive by its final -e (instead of -a) and the absence of a tense marker like -na- or -li-.

quiz.question: What ending marks the Swahili subjunctive?
Which sentence uses the subjunctive correctly for 'Let's go'?

lessons.title: Perfect Tense (-me-)
lessons.explanation: The Swahili perfect tense uses the infix -me- to show a completed action with present relevance, similar to English 'have done': Nimemaliza (I have finished). This contrasts with -li-, which states a simple past fact without emphasizing its current result.
examples: Nimemaliza kazi. — I have finished the work.
Amefika. — He/she has arrived.
Tumesoma kitabu hiki. — We have read this book.
Bado hajala. — He/she hasn't eaten yet. (negative perfect)
lessons.tip: Use -me- when the past action still matters right now; use -li- for a plain, finished past event.

quiz.question: Which infix marks the Swahili perfect tense ('have done')?
What does 'Amefika' mean?

lessons.title: Relative Clauses (-enye, -o, -cho infixes)
lessons.explanation: Swahili forms relative clauses ('that/which/who') with a class-agreeing infix inserted into the verb, rather than a separate relative pronoun. For the KI-/VI- class, '-cho-' marks 'which': kitabu ninachosoma ('the book that I am reading') = ki-tabu ni-na-cho-soma.
examples: Kitabu ninachosoma ni kizuri. — The book that I am reading is good.
Mtu ninayemwona ni rafiki yangu. — The person whom I see is my friend.
Watu wanaocheza ni wanafunzi. — The people who are playing are students.
Nyumba niliyoijenga ni kubwa. — The house that I built is big.
lessons.tip: The relative infix (-cho-, -ye-, -o-, -yo-, etc.) always matches the noun class of what's being referred to — this is one of Swahili's most distinctive advanced features.

quiz.question: How does Swahili typically form a relative clause like 'the book that I am reading'?
options: With a separate relative pronoun before the verb
With a class-agreeing infix inserted into the verb

lessons.title: Passive Voice (-wa suffix)
lessons.explanation: Swahili verbs form the passive by inserting -w- (or -liwa/-lewa for some stems) before the final vowel: soma (read) becomes somwa (be read); penda (love) becomes pendwa (be loved). The agent, if mentioned, is introduced with na ('by').
examples: Kitabu kinasomwa. — The book is being read.
Chakula kilipikwa na mama. — The food was cooked by mother.
Barua itaandikwa kesho. — The letter will be written tomorrow.
Mlango ulifunguliwa. — The door was opened.
lessons.tip: Insert -w- right before the final vowel of the verb stem to make it passive; use na to introduce the agent.

quiz.question: How is the Swahili passive typically formed?
Which word introduces the agent ('by ___') in a Swahili passive sentence?

lessons.title: Applicative and Causative Verb Extensions
lessons.explanation: Swahili verbs can be extended with suffixes that change their meaning. The applicative -ia/-ea adds 'for/to/on behalf of': andika (write) becomes andikia (write for/to someone). The causative -isha/-esha adds 'cause to': -jua (know) becomes -julisha (introduce, cause to know).
examples: Ninamwandikia barua. — I am writing a letter to/for him.
Alinipikia chakula. — She cooked food for me. (applicative)
Nitamjulisha rafiki yangu. — I will introduce my friend. (causative, from -jua)
Mwalimu alisomesha wanafunzi. — The teacher made the students read/taught them. (causative)
lessons.tip: Applicative (-ia/-ea) answers 'for/to whom'; causative (-isha/-esha) answers 'who made it happen.' Both attach before the final vowel.

quiz.question: What does the applicative extension -ia/-ea typically add to a verb's meaning?
Which extension marks the causative ('cause to ___')?

lessons.title: Stative Extension (-ika/-eka)
lessons.explanation: The stative (neuter) extension -ika or -eka attaches before the final vowel of a verb to express that something is capable of happening, or ends up in a resulting state, without naming an agent: vunja (break something) becomes vunjika (get broken/be breakable); soma (read) becomes someka (be readable).
examples: Kikombe kimevunjika. — The cup is broken/has broken. (no agent named)
Kitabu hiki kinasomeka vizuri. — This book reads well/is readable.
Mlango umefungika. — The door has gotten shut/is shut.
Tatizo hili linaeleweka. — This problem is understandable.
lessons.tip: Stative -ika/-eka differs from passive -wa: passive implies someone did it (even if unnamed), while stative describes a resulting state or inherent possibility, with no agent implied at all.

quiz.question: What does the stative extension -ika/-eka typically express?
options: A resulting state or possibility, without an agent

quiz.question: What does 'Kikombe kimevunjika' mean?
options: Someone broke the cup on purpose
The cup is being broken by someone
